Abstract

In this work we have used Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy and Spectroscopy to learn about the electronic structure of molecules at metal surfaces and about their effect on the plasmonic properties of the optical nanocavity between the tip and the sample of the STM. For the last purpose, we collect the light emitted by the junction due to tunnel electroluminescence. This technique is usually the so-called Scanning Tunneling Microscopy Induced Light Emission (STM-LE). Regarding the characterization of the electronic structure, we have investigated D~5h~(I)-C~90~ fullertube molecules on Au(111), Ag(111) and NaCl/Ag(111). Fullertubes are an emerging new nanoform of carbon with structures that are part nanotube, part fullerene. Recently, researchers have been able to produce them in large enough quantities to allow for sublimation onto metal surfaces and a subsequent STM investigation.

seccion: Abstract
texto:
Abstract

Fullertubes are an emerging new nanoform of carbon with structures that are part nanotube, part fullerene. Recently, researchers have been able to produce them in large enough quantities to allow for sublimation onto metal surfaces and a subsequent STM investigation. We have experimentally characterized their molecular orbitals (MOs) for the first time by STM on the previous metallic surfaces. These investigations have allowed us to distinguish two kinds of MOs. First, those MOs arising from quantum confinement of electrons in the valence or conduction bands of CNTs, which we call Carbon Nanotube (CNT)-like. Second, those whose symmetry properties do not exhibit the five-fold azimuthal symmetry characteristic of CNT bands, which we call fullerene-like MOs. We believe that this classification is very important to tailor the properties of this exciting new molecules.

seccion: Abstract
texto:
Abstract

In this Thesis, we have characterized the energies and spatial extension of their MOs by spatially resolved dI/dV maps. As expected, the electroluminescence spectra show basically a plasmonic character, instead of molecular emission. By comparing the electroluminescence spectra with the tip placed on top of a molecule or in a metallic area, we observe that the raw intensity is significantly smaller on the molecules. However, a normalization procedure to eliminate electronic structure factors removes mostly this effect. This procedure, however, allows for the observation of subtle changes in the spectral distribution of the plasmonic modes. We attribute these changes to the existence of new optical transitions between the electrons of the metal substrate and new interface states formed around the position of the molecules. Finally, we searched for new ways to characterize the optical transitions within organic molecules adsorbed on metal surfaces.

Finally, we searched for new ways to characterize the optical transitions within organic molecules adsorbed on metal surfaces. We have repeated the experiments with a different kind of molecules that present a 3D structure that allows for a separation between their MOs and the metal states. The investigated molecules are metalated tetraphenyl porphyrins (TPPs), some of which, show out-of-plane dipole moments to strengthen plasmon-exciton interaction. A similar approach as the one followed for the BPEA and BPEN molecules reveals spectral features in the plasmonic spectra that we can correlate to the absorption spectra of the molecules. Thus, we believe to have found a method to obtain optical information of organic molecules directly adsorbed on metal surfaces.

Chapter 1: Introduction > 1.1 Motivation

The interaction between electromagnetic radiation and electric charges, represents a crucial mater in many fields in science and technology. Biological processes such as light-harvesting and photosynthesis originates from charge separation by photon adsorption. Scientific tools and everyday commercial devices like light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and stimulated sources (LASERs) work by emitting photons due to charge recombination. Previous studies on photon excitations of electronic systems on solid-state materials at the atomic scale revealed properties of single molecules that have not been observable in its ensembles structures [1]. Furthermore, light-matter interaction at nanostructures has gained much scientific interest as the development of new devices for future quantum information technologies arises [2][3].

Chapter 1: Introduction > 1.1 Motivation

Previous studies on photon excitations of electronic systems on solid-state materials at the atomic scale revealed properties of single molecules that have not been observable in its ensembles structures [1]. Furthermore, light-matter interaction at nanostructures has gained much scientific interest as the development of new devices for future quantum information technologies arises [2][3]. The term light-matter interaction refers to the coupling between the excited states in quantum emitters (QEs), such as single molecules, organic nanocrystals, or organic quantum dots, and the optical radiation modes. These modes can also be enhanced by confining the light to nanoscale metallic cavities which bear plasmonic resonances. When this interaction is relatively weak, so that the excitons in the quantum emitter and the optical modes of the cavity retain its character, we say that we are in the weak coupling regime.

These modes can also be enhanced by confining the light to nanoscale metallic cavities which bear plasmonic resonances. When this interaction is relatively weak, so that the excitons in the quantum emitter and the optical modes of the cavity retain its character, we say that we are in the weak coupling regime. In this regime, the most notorious effect is the enhancement of the electromagnetic field to the plasmonic modes of the cavity. Thus, leading to applications such as single molecule sensors [4] or to enhance the radiation rate by the Purcell factor [5]. For stronger interactions, both the excited states of the QE and the optical modes hybridize and are no longer purely matter or purely radiation. As the enhancement of the electromagnetic modes due to the plasmonic resonances of the cavity is larger for smaller cavity size, strong coupling usually requires that the optical resonator's size is similar to the QEs' [6][7].

Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM) has demonstrated to be a powerful experimental technique to study the optical and electronic properties of metallic, semiconducting nanostructures and single molecule systems. STM allows us to study the electroluminescence induced by the tunnelling current and quantum size phenomena on these systems with a spatial resolution of the order of picometers. To reach such spatial resolution the STM overcomes the Abbe diffraction limit by its sharp metallic tip that acts as a metallic structure of subwavelength dimensions which allow an efficient coupling between electromagnetic near-field and far-field radiation [1]. Chapter 1:Introduction The tip-sample gap on an STM behaves as a plasmonic nanocavity due to the spatial confinement of the electromagnetic field inside the tunnel junction, the local character of the excitation current as an excitation source and the small distance between the tip and the sample of the STM. As a difference with other plasmonic nanocavities, the one formed by an STM can be tuned in different ways. We can control the tip-sample distance with sub-angstrom precision due to the piezo electric positioning system. Thus, we can control the coupling's strength between the excitonic modes of the QEs and plasmonic modes of the cavity. We can also change the applied bias voltage to change the weight of the energy distribution of the LSPR by accessing from solely low energy modes at low bias voltage to the full spectrum at higher bias voltages.

Thus, we can control the coupling's strength between the excitonic modes of the QEs and plasmonic modes of the cavity. We can also change the applied bias voltage to change the weight of the energy distribution of the LSPR by accessing from solely low energy modes at low bias voltage to the full spectrum at higher bias voltages. Finally, we can reshape the apex of the tip, being able to detune the LSPR from the frequencies of QEs and hence, changing the plasmonic response of the nanojunction. For these reasons, STM can become a unique tool for the study of the optical and electronic properties for systems that present coupling between their plasmonic and excitonic modes. STM has proven to be a great experimental technique in many fields. To briefly name some of them we have: superconductive materials [12], surface chemistry [13][14], catalysis [15] and biomedicine [16].

seccion: Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics
texto:
Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics

Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics In this chapter we first give a brief introduction about the fundamentals of plasmonics describing the differences between bulk plasmons, surface plasmons (SP) and localized surface plasmons (LSP). Then we describe some of the applications of the LSPs due to their radiative decay, in the field of modern Nanoscience. We continue describing the fundamental aspects of the physics of the STM, such as the direction of the tunnelling current with respect the bias voltage, the quantum tunnelling effect which constitute the basis of the workings of the STM and the Tersoff and Hamann Model to describe the tunnelling current (I~t~) through a vacuum barrier between a real solid surface and a model probe. Furthermore, we introduce a model to determine the proportionality of the Local Density of States (LDOS) with I~t~ and the elastic and inelastic transitions of tunnelling electrons showing how can they be distinguished by Scanning Tunnelling Spectroscopy (STS).

Then, we describe how the STM allows us to access the light emitted to the far field from the nanocavities with the technique so-called, Scanning Tunnelling Microscope Induced Light Emission (STM-LE). Afterwards, with the electroluminescence spectra and the inelastic ratio, we introduce a normalization procedure that separates the electronic structure from the Optical Radiative Density (Purcell Factor).

seccion: Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.1 Introduction to plasmonics
texto:
Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.1 Introduction to plasmonics

In 1952, David Pines and David Bohm, to explain energy losses of fast electrons passing through metallic foils, they discussed a quantized bulk plasma oscillation of electrons in metals which they called "plasmon" [21] [22]. Plasmons can be described as collective charge-density oscillations coupled to electromagnetic field oscillations quantized with an associated quasiparticle of energy $\hslash\omega_{p}$. This means, considering the atomic nucleus of atoms in a metal as fixed, we can define plasmons as an oscillation of electron density [21]. In Figure 2.1 a, we show an schematic representation of a bulk plasmon: When applying an external electric field, pointing down in Figure 2.1 a, electrons will move to the upper side of the metal until cancelling the influence of the electric field inside the bulk, populating the upper part and leaving the bulk below with unscreened positive ions corresponding to the nucleus of the metal.

In Figure 2.1 a, we show an schematic representation of a bulk plasmon: When applying an external electric field, pointing down in Figure 2.1 a, electrons will move to the upper side of the metal until cancelling the influence of the electric field inside the bulk, populating the upper part and leaving the bulk below with unscreened positive ions corresponding to the nucleus of the metal. This creates a difference in the surface charge density of the bulk, negative above it ($\sigma = - neu$) and positive below ($\sigma = + neu$). If we took out the electric field this electron density will try to come back to its original state due to the electron-electron repulsion and electron-positive ions attraction, creating an oscillation at a plasma frequency until it loses the energy by ohmic losses or other damping mechanisms. These oscillations, when quantized are the so-called bulk plasmons [22].

Similarly, when the perturbation of the charge density occurs periodically along a metal-dielectric interface we have the so-called Surface Plasmons (SP), predicted in 1957 by Rufus Ritchie [23]. They are coherent delocalized electron oscillations that move along the interface generating, thus, evanescent electromagnetic fields inside, and outside the metal [21] [23]. These waves involve the displacement of the charge density on the metal and electromagnetic perturbation taking place in the dielectric medium of the interface [21]. They are called Surface Plasmon Polaritons (SPP), illustrated in Figure 2.1 b. The physics of Localized Surface Plasmons have proven its utility on many applications, mostly based in the enormous enhancement factor for the electromagnetic field in the presence of LSPs, which can reach values of 10^5^. This enhancement leads to important effects when placing quantum emitters (single molecules, quantum dots) in such a strong field. In this section we compile some of the most relevant examples. *Single-Molecule plasmon-based sensing*: By placing a quantum emitter such as a molecule in a plasmonic nanocavity or nearby a metallic nanoparticle, the energy of the plasmonic response can shift, thus enabling to track these shifts with respect time. In Figure 2.2 a [26], a single nanorod of gold functionalized with biotin has been inserted in an environment that presents the desired protein to track. When the protein binds to the receptors, the plasmonic emission redshifts.

In Figure 2.2 a [26], a single nanorod of gold functionalized with biotin has been inserted in an environment that presents the desired protein to track. When the protein binds to the receptors, the plasmonic emission redshifts. This behavior in the plasmonic response allows to track in time when there has been a change in population of the proteins attached to the gold nanorod, see Figure 2.2 b. In that graph, the sudden and stepwise dependence of the intensity fluctuation do not correspond to macroscopic fluctuations, which would be smoother in time. They must rather arise from the adsorption or desorption of individual molecules (or at least a small number of them). The fact that a single molecule can affect the LSP so much that it can produce a macroscopic observable effect, and hence, allowing single-molecule sensing, is closely related to the strong amplification of the electric fields around the metallic nanoparticle.

This physical phenomenon is the so-called Purcell effect, discovered by Edward Mills Purcell in 1945 [27]. According to Fermi's golden rule, the spontaneous emission rate of a quantum emitter initially excited in state *i* to relax to the ground state, *f*, $\Gamma_{i \rightarrow f}\$is proportional to the density of final states ${\rho(E}_{f})$, following the expression (1): $$\Gamma_{i \rightarrow f} = \ \frac{2\pi}{\hslash}\left| M_{if} \right|^{2}{\rho(E}_{f})$$   (1) where $M_{if}$ is the tunnelling matrix element between the initial and final state. In a nanocavity with LSP modes, the high electromagnetic fields enhance the number of final states ${\rho(E}_{f})$ with respect to the vacuum. Thus, Fermi's Golden Rule predicts that the emission rate will be higher when the quantum emitter is close to a plasmonic nanostructure than free in the vacuum, and thus, luminescence intensities would also be higher.

The principal aim of this thesis is to study the optoelectronic properties of plasmonic nanocavities conformed by a metallic tip and a substrate that can be a noble metallic surface (Ag(111) or Au(111)) or a dielectric material (NaCl) on the previous metallic surfaces. For the realization of our experiments, we employed a Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM). An STM is a Microscope that uses the tunnelling electrons between an atomically sharp tip and a metal surface to obtain atomic resolution images of molecules or surfaces. STM has also revealed itself as a very versatile tool, capable not only of imaging surfaces with atomic or molecular resolution, but also to map their electronic structure, manipulate matter at the atomic scale, obtain information about the structure of their magnetic domains or, as we will stress in this thesis, to obtain atomically resolved information on the optical response of surfaces and molecules supported on them.

The Quantum Tunnelling Effect is the basic principle underlying of the working of an STM. The Quantum Tunnelling Effect is a quantum mechanical phenomenon in which a particle with energy E travels through a potential barrier of energy $U_{0}$ of width L, being $E < U_{0}$ as depicted in Figure 2.5. Classically, to cross the barrier, the energy E of the particle should be $E \geq U_{0}$. However, in quantum mechanics, the particle's wavefunction does not vanish in the classically forbidden region but becomes an evanescent wave. Indeed, solving the 1D time independent Schrödinger equation for the particle of this problem gives a finite probability of transmission through the potential barrier. For a potential barrier $U_{0}$ of a certain length L, the wavefunction of a particle with an energy E such that $E < U_{0}$, decays exponentially. However, there is a probability that part of the wavefunction locates at the other side of the barrier and, hence, the particle. This means that some particles with $E < U_{0}$ can "tunnel" through the potential barrier towards the other side. To obtain the probability of finding the electron in the barrier potential (region II) we need to solve the 1D time independent Schrödinger equation below. $$\left\lbrack - \frac{\hslash^{2}}{2m}\frac{d^{2}}{{dx}^{2}} + U(x) \right\rbrack\varphi(x) = E\varphi(x)$$   (4) Here, E represents the electron energy and U(x) the one-dimensional potential depicted in Figure 2.5 ($U_{0}$). As the potential barrier divides the space in three regions, we must solve the Schrödinger equation for each one.

Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.3 Fundamentals of STM > 2.3.2 Direction of tunnelling current vs. sign of the bias voltage

Figure 2.6 shows a schematic representation of the energy level alignment of tip and sample under the application of different bias voltages. When the applied voltage is zero, as the tip and the sample are in contact through the electronics of the STM, the Fermi levels of both electrodes remain aligned (see Figure 2.6 a). Because most tunnelling processes are elastic, to establish a sizeable current, it is necessary that occupied states in one electrode have the same energy as the empty states of the other electrode. The alignment of the Fermi levels in the case of zero bias voltage, thus, implies that no tunnelling can occur between tip and sample. However, if we apply a bias voltage, the Fermi levels of the tip and the sample shift exactly by the voltage applied to the junction. As shown in Figure 2.6 b, for positive bias voltages, there is an energy window in which we find both occupied states of the tip and unoccupied levels of the sample.

Although the electrons do not have enough energy to overcome the potential energy barrier (related to tip and sample work functions) that exist between the tip and the sample, they travel through the vacuum barrier via quantum tunnelling. Thus, a tunnel current establishes between occupied states of the tip and unoccupied states in the sample. For negative bias voltages, the dealignment of the Fermi levels is reversed with respect to positive voltages, and the tunnel current flows from occupied states of the sample into unoccupied states of the tip (See Figure 2.6 c).

As the wave function decay exponentially in the vacuum barrier, we can establish the relation of $\rho_{s}({{\overrightarrow{r}}_{0},E}_{F}) \propto e^{- 2\kappa(R + d)}$ which leaves the expression of $I_{T}$ as $$I_{T} \propto V_{bias}e^{- 2\kappa d}$$                          (15) This resulting expression is very useful to easily determine the behavior of the tunnelling current for changes on the voltage gap and the tip to sample distance. For the former, the tunnelling current is proportional to the bias voltage and for the later, $I_{T}$ decays exponentially with the tip-sample distance. Despite the insights offered by the Tersoff-Hamann model, it is important to keep in mind that its many approximations limit they predictive power to understand aspects as important as the capability of STM to perform spectroscopy, which we will describe below.

One of the capabilities of the STM is to probe the Local Density of States (LDOS) for occupied an empty states in the same experiment. These measurements allow us to study the conduction and valence bands in the same system. As the tip of the STM is a mobile electrode, we can track both the energy dependence of the LDOS and its spatial dependence with atomic resolution. The measurement of the LDOS arises from the proportionality between its value and the derivative of the tunnelling current. Since we need to describe the dependence of the tunnel current with relatively large voltages, we will need to explore a territory that is beyond the Tersoff and Hamann model described above. In the work of N. Lang [36], they generalize the equation (13), obtaining the following expression, valid for low temperatures. $$I_{T} \propto \int_{0}^{eV}{dE\rho_{t}(E - eV)\rho_{s}({\overrightarrow{r}}_{0},E)}$$   (16)

We previously mentioned that not all states have the same probability to tunnel through the vacuum barrier. For example, for electronic levels with higher energies $E$, the transmission factor $T$ increases with the energy of the electronic states. So, the contribution of high energy states to the tunnelling current will be larger than that corresponding to energies far from the vacuum level. Moreover, electronic states with lower $k_{\parallel}$ values (coming from the states at the center of the Brillouin zone) contribute more to the tunnel current, as they have a higher transmission factor $T$. Considering a featureless DOS of the tip and a weak energy dependence of $T$, we can obtain the LDOS of the sample by calculating the derivative of equation (18). This calculus leads to the following expression which shows that the derivative of the tunnelling current with respect the energy is directly proportional to the LDOS of the sample.

texto:
Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.3 Fundamentals of STM > 2.3.5 Elastic and Inelastic tunnelling transitions

All the analysis that we have shown so far imply that the tunnelling processes are elastic, i.e. that the energy of the initial and final states is the same during a tunnel process. However researchers have established, and is very relevant for the interpretation of the luminescence experiments shown in this thesis, that when the system presents elementary excitations (vibrational, spin-flip, plasmons, etc....), a small fraction of electrons can undergo inelastic tunnelling processes, in which the energy of the final state is lower than that of the initial state, and the difference in energy goes to creating an elementary excitation (see Figure 2.7 a). Inelastic tunnelling has a subtle but measurable impact on the measured STS spectra.

Inelastic tunnelling has a subtle but measurable impact on the measured STS spectra. Such effects can be understood by inspecting the schematic representation of Figure 2.7 b which shows that the dependence of the inelastic contribution to the tunnel current follows a function of the bias voltage for an inelastic process of energy $\hslash\omega$. Such contribution will be null until we reach a bias voltage that corresponds to the excitation energy $\pm \hslash\omega$/e. Increasing the absolute value of the bias voltage above this threshold also increases the number of possible inelastic processes. Thus, the current not only shows a jump at the energy of the excitation but also a monotonous increase with voltage. We can observe this increase in the kink that the tunnelling current displays at the voltage corresponding to $\pm \hslash\omega/e$. These kinks translate in the dI/dV curve as two conductance steps.

In 1976 J. Lambe and S. L. McCarthy discovered that when a current flows through a tunnel junction it can emit light [39]. In their work, they used metal-insulator-metal tunnel junctions to investigate the electroluminescence produced by the injection of a tunnel current. They interpreted this effect in terms of inelastic tunnelling excitation of localized surface plasmon modes, existing due to the rugosity of the metal-insulator interface. A few years later, and after the invention of the STM, J.K. Gimzewski and co-workers [40][41] reported light emission from a tunnel junction of an STM in metallic samples and with metallic tips. They attributed that light emission to the existence of LSPR modes in the gap between the tip and the sample excited by inelastic tunnel events. Ho and co-workers visualized the Fermi's golden rule through atomic-scale spatial imaging of 1D chains of Ag atoms. They obtained photon images with the STM by varying the bias voltage to control tunnelling electrons and the radiative transition in inelastic tunnelling [44]. To correctly understand their spectra, they had to consider the electronic factors that contemplate the abundance of initial and final electronic states for the inelastic transitions. However, it was not clear the estimation of this factor. There is relative difficulty to reproduce the same spectrum between different tips. This difficulty plus the uncertainty about the role of electronic states of tip and sample in the spectra, has difficulted the exploitation of such technique in nanoplasmonic's.

This difficulty plus the uncertainty about the role of electronic states of tip and sample in the spectra, has difficulted the exploitation of such technique in nanoplasmonic's. Even though, this technique promises many exciting discoveries as the plasmonic cavity associated to the tunnel junction is tunable. In recent years, light emission from STM has gained a renewed interest, due to the following discovery. When a quantum emitter is on top of a thin dielectric layer, the injection of tunnel current can induce excitonic emission [45][46][47][48][49]. The mechanism for such emission has remained long debated in the literature. Now, explanations seem to be converging towards the role of intermediate hot electrons rather than inelastic tunnelling, as our group, among others, first proposed in the literature [50][17]. However, in this thesis we are going to focus mostly on plasmonic emission due to inelastic tunnelling. Due to this, we postpone further discussion until necessary.

Figure 2.9 a, shows a schematic representation of an electron tunnelling inelastically from the tip to the substrate emitting a photon of energy $\hslash\omega$, equal to the difference in energy from the occupied state (tip) to the unoccupied one (substrate). We can easily obtain $I_{t}^{el}(V_{bias}^{*})$ experimentally by recording the I(V) curve at the same stabilization conditions than the luminescence spectrum. This density of optical states arises in plasmonic nanocavities as a continuous distribution of the plasmonic modes with respect the energy. As shown in Equation (22), this product separates the electronic effects in $I_{t}\left( {eV}_{bias} - \hslash\omega \right)$ and the optical information in $D_{r}(\hslash\omega)$ with its validity for restricted to $\hslash\omega < {eV}_{bias} - O\left( k_{B}T \right)$. [32]

As we saw in section 4.2, the main advantage of this normalization procedure is that we can extract exclusively the optical information $D_{r}(\hslash\omega)$ and do so experimentally. Figure 2.12 a shows one example of how the procedure works: three I(V) curves taken at a stabilization current of $I_{t}^{st} = 0.47\ nA$ and stabilization bias voltages of $V_{bias}^{st}$: 2.9 V (red line), 3.3 V (black line), 3.7 V (blue line). Right after taking one $I_{t}(V)$ curve, we take the light spectrum $I_{l}\left( \hslash\omega,V_{bias}^{st} \right)$ at the same stabilization voltage, see Figure 2.12 b. Now we have all the information needed for the normalization. Figure 2.12 b, also depicts the $R_{inel}\left( \hslash\omega,V_{bias} \right)$'s obtained from $I_{t}(V)$'s following the procedure explained in the previous section. Finally, we can normalize the spectra by using Equation (23), and obtain the Optical Radiative Density $D_{r}(\hslash\omega)$ (The Purcell Factor).

The normalization procedure described above has proven useful to understand many different aspects of STM-induced plasmonic luminescence, from the role of atomic-scale defects [11], to the switching behavior between plasmonic and excitonic luminescence in C~60~ nano islands on NaCl/Ag(111) [50]. This section depicts other consequence of our analysis related to the so-called overbias emission, and how it opens a new way to determine electronic temperatures. Overbias emission is the phenomenon for which we can obtain some light at energies above the applied bias voltage, that is, above the quantum cut-off. The quantum cut-off is thus not perfectly sharp, and this opens the question as to what functional form should have the cut-off function and which are the parameters that determine it. Figure 2.13 shows an example of the overbias emission effect [53].

Previous literature offers two possible explanations for the overbias emission. The first one is thermal broadening effects. The inelastic processes from electrons in the nanojunction increase the electronic temperature making it higher than the lattice temperature. This leads to blackbody radiation from the hot electron gas, which would explain the overbias emission. [54][55][56]. However, to obtain quantitative agreement with the experimental data we require several thousand Kelvin of temperature.

[54][55][56]. However, to obtain quantitative agreement with the experimental data we require several thousand Kelvin of temperature. The second explanation is the existence of two-electron processes in which part of the energy of a first tunnelling electron transfer to a second one. That extra energy allows the excitation of plasmon modes with more energy than the bias voltage, and hence, overbias emission. [57][58][59][60]. The observed quadratic dependence of the overbias intensity with the tunnelling current supports this model. Both explanations seem contradictory and the discrepancies between both models represent a problem for finding one that accurately measures the electronic temperature of the tunnel junction. In our work of [53], we established connections between these two models for overbias emission and demonstrated that we can accurately measure the electronic temperature of the tunnel junction.

The characterization revealed that for junction temperatures above 30 K and tunnel currents of tens of nanoamperes thermal broadening effects are enough to explain overbias emission. However, for lower junction temperatures and higher tunnelling currents, there is a big difference between the nominal junction temperature and the electronic temperature obtained from the overbias intensities. These two observations suggest a two-electron mechanism where the first electron excites the system, and the second one tests the thermalization of the system by the time it tunnels. With this work, we applied the normalization procedure to end up establishing some connections between the first two explanations from the previous literature and accurately determine the electronic temperature of the system.

seccion: Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.5 Conclusions
texto:
Chapter 2: Fundamentals of STM Plasmonics > 2.5 Conclusions

In conclusion, the STM presents a promising tool for the study of the LSPR. Also, its picometre resolution allows us to study the effects that defects of atomic size or molecules located inside the tunnel nanojunction may cause in the plasmonic effects. However, previous studies on the plasmonic effects on an STM did not consider the electronic structure of the system which represents a drawback to comprehend the effect of molecules or atomic size defects in the plasmonic modes. The purpose of this thesis is to study the LSPR with the STM, exploiting the normalization developed to take out the electronic structure of the system and end up solely with the purely optical effects of these atomic or nanometric structures in the plasmonic modes.

seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up

Experimental Set-up We carried out all the experiments using an Ultra High Vacuum (UHV) Low Temperature (LT) Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) or as it will be called in the rest of the manuscript LT-STM. The STM also has an external optical set up attached to collect and measure the light emitted from the plasmonic nanojunction between the tip and the sample. We refer to this combination of STM and optical instrumentation as the Photon STM. This chapter describes the instrumentation used for the realization of the experiments and is divided in different sections describing the UHV chamber, the STM, sample preparation procedures and the light detection system.

Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.1 Ultra High Vacuum System

The purpose of our experiments is to study the optical and electronic properties of organic molecules on different surfaces. To do that, the top layers of the substrate must be flat and clean at the atomic scale. To ensure an atomically clean sample for an extended period of time during in which we record the measurements, we need to work at very low gas pressures. We can use the Kinetic Theory of Gases to estimate the flux of particles for a certain gas that crosses an area over time yielding: $$F = \frac{P}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_{B}T}}$$                (25) Being F, the flux of particles, P, the pressure, m, the mass of an individual gas molecule, k~B~, the Boltzmann constant and T, the temperature.

$$F = \frac{P}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_{B}T}}$$                (25) Being F, the flux of particles, P, the pressure, m, the mass of an individual gas molecule, k~B~, the Boltzmann constant and T, the temperature. For the conditions of air at Room Temperature (RT $\sim$ 300 K) and assuming, as the earth atmosphere is 78 % N~2~, that we can estimate the mass of an individual molecule as the mass of N~2~ (28 a.m.u.), we can substitute these values obtaining the following relation of the flux of particles with respect the pressure P. $$F \approx 3 \times \ 10^{20} \times P(mbar)$$           (26) For a High Vacuum pressure of 10^-6^ mbar, the number of gas molecules per square meter per second is approximately 3 x 10^14^ (particles/(m^2^ x s)). On the other hand, the density of surface atoms is also of the order to 10^14^ atoms/m^2^. Thus, contaminant gas molecules will cover the surface in seconds for even High Vacuum.

seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.3 Pumping stages for UHV
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.3 Pumping stages for UHV

For reaching UHV we need to set up a pumping system, including pumps with different capabilities on the Preparation and STM chambers described in the previous paragraph. Although a valve separates the STM chamber and the Preparation chamber to be independently pumped by ionic pumps, we usually carry out the first two steps of this procedure with the valve between them open. - First, we make a rough vacuum on the chambers of down to 10^-3^ mbar by using a nXDS scroll pump from EDWARDS. One fixed and one orbiting scroll conforms this pump. Voids at the inlet of the vacuum pump occur due to the orbiting scroll moving within the fixed scroll. The rotation of the scroll compresses and transports the pumped gas from the entrance, through the spaces in between both scrolls to the center of the fixed scroll where it is expulsed [61]. - After reaching 10^-3^ mbar, we turn on the turbomolecular pump from PFEIFFER Vacuum.

The rotation of the scroll compresses and transports the pumped gas from the entrance, through the spaces in between both scrolls to the center of the fixed scroll where it is expulsed [61]. - After reaching 10^-3^ mbar, we turn on the turbomolecular pump from PFEIFFER Vacuum. The entrance of this pump connects to the Preparation chamber and, the exit of the pump, to the entrance of the scroll pump. This pump employs multiple stages of pairs of a stationary stator blade and a rotating motor blade of frequency of 820 Hz (1000 Hz for the Load-Lock chamber which we will describe in section 3.6). This multiple pairs form an axial compressor. By repeated collision with the rotor blade, the gas molecules receive a momentum on a certain direction. The turbomolecular pump creates and holds the vacuum by pushing the molecules from the entrance of the pump towards its exit. With this, we lower the pressure of the chambers below 10^-8^ mbar [62].

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.3 Pumping stages for UHV

The turbomolecular pump creates and holds the vacuum by pushing the molecules from the entrance of the pump towards its exit. With this, we lower the pressure of the chambers below 10^-8^ mbar [62]. - At this point, we need to accelerate the desorption processes of gas molecules adsorbed on the walls of the chambers. This is done by a bake-out system that heats the chambers for usually 24 hours (200 °C for the Preparation Chamber and 133.7 °C for the STM chamber). - Finally, we reach the UHV pressure of 10^-11^ mbar in the STM chamber and 10^-10^ mbar in the Preparation chamber by ionic pumps from Gamma Vacuum in each chamber. The ionic pump presents two elements, an anode and a chemically active cathode of Ti. The ionic pump ionizes the gas that goes through the anode by an electrical potential of 7 kV and accelerates it towards the chemically active cathode. This causes two possibilities; the ionized particles can sputter the cathode, or they can stick to the cathode.

Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.3 Pumping stages for UHV

The ionic pump ionizes the gas that goes through the anode by an electrical potential of 7 kV and accelerates it towards the chemically active cathode. This causes two possibilities; the ionized particles can sputter the cathode, or they can stick to the cathode. If they sputter the cathode, the chemically active cathode material traps the gas molecules and evacuates it by chemisorption or physisorption. For inert and lighter gases such as He or H~2~ they tend to stick to the cathode and get adsorbed by physisorption. Also, some ions can become neutral by the cathode, in this case, the ionic pump presents exposed surfaces to bury these particles [63].

The STM Chamber, as mentioned before hosts the Omicron LT-STM head where we do all the measurements. However, it also presents some other instrumentation that is worth mentioning after entering on the insides of the LT-STM head. In this section we describe the principal parts of the STM chamber, the exterior of the chamber in Figure 3.2 a and its interior in Figure 3.2 b. We numbered and highlighted these parts on both figures for better visualization. - The STM lever (1 red): it allows to place the Omicron LT-STM head in three different positions by controlling the elongations of the springs of the head. The first position is the contact mode where the LT-STM head is in full thermal contact with the bottom of the cryostat. This allows the fastest cooling of the substrate. Secondly, we have the standby position. It is similar to the previous position but with the LT-STM head in contact but not pressed towards the bottom of the cryostat.

- The evaporator for cold deposition (4 green): it is a cone crucible evaporator purchased from SPECS. The purpose of an evaporator at the STM chamber is depositing molecules on samples while they sit in the STM and, thus, it enables deposition at low temperatures, where the diffusion of the molecules is less than at room temperature (RT). This allows for the study of individual molecules that otherwise would self-assemble into islands. The evaporator was labeled as "in cold" as it evaporates the molecules on "cold" samples [65]. To reach the low temperature regime (in our case, the liquid Helium (LHe) evaporation temperature, 4.4 K), we have a cryogenic system formed by two concentric cryostats inside the STM. The outer cryostat shown in Figure 3.2 b (5 blue), is usually filled with liquid Nitrogen (LN~2~). Although it cools the sample at the LN~2~ temperature (77 K), the main purpose of the exterior cryostat is to act as a thermal shield for the inner cryostat.

The outer cryostat shown in Figure 3.2 b (5 blue), is usually filled with liquid Nitrogen (LN~2~). Although it cools the sample at the LN~2~ temperature (77 K), the main purpose of the exterior cryostat is to act as a thermal shield for the inner cryostat. Thus, the liquid from the inner cryostat evaporates at a slower rate, holding the sample at low temperature for larger periods of time. Depending on the temperature we want to measure, we can fill the inner cryostat with LN~2~ (77 K) or LHe (4.4 K). A LakeShore 325 temperature controller measures this temperature by means of a Si diode [66]. When filling with LHe (4.4 K), there is also a Helium Depth Indicator from Twickenham Scientific Instruments that allows us to measure the level of LHe inside the inner cryostat [67]. The STM chamber hosts the Omicron LT-STM head at the bottom of the cryostats and inside two rotating thermal shields (6 orange), each one in thermal contact with one of the cryostats.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.1 Working schematics of an STM

As we mentioned in Chapter 2 the working principle of the STM as shown in Figure 3.3 is the quantum tunnelling effect of the electrons. The effect establishes a tunnelling current after the dealignment of the Fermi levels between the tip and the substrate, reached by applying a bias voltage. The probe electrode is a sharp metallic tip. We bring the termination of such tip, ideally a single atom, to a nanometric scale distance of the sample by piezoelectric stack motors. Moreover, we control the fine position by using a piezoelectric tube, with metal coatings allowing for x, y and z motions. The substrate must be a metallic or heavily doped semiconductor surface to facilitate electron transport. Then, as mentioned above, the preamplifier converts the tunnelling current measured in the tunnel junction into a voltage signal and sends it to the MATRIX electronic controller [68].

The substrate must be a metallic or heavily doped semiconductor surface to facilitate electron transport. Then, as mentioned above, the preamplifier converts the tunnelling current measured in the tunnel junction into a voltage signal and sends it to the MATRIX electronic controller [68]. To measure at constant tunnelling current, the software compares the actual current signal with respect a current setpoint by the feedback loop. The feedback then, retracts or approaches the tip to maintain the set tunnelling current. It is possible to measure without the feedback loop, measuring instead of the changes in the tip-sample distance, the tunnelling current. We do all the STM measurements of the samples on an Omicron LT-STM head, see Figure 3.4. The STM head is inside both the exterior and interior rotating thermal shields and below the inner cryostat. In this section, we describe the principal parts of the Omicron STM head which are numbered and highlighted in color for a better visualization. - Sample stage (1, green): located at the bottom of the cryostat we have the sample stage. Two black rails form the sample stage creating a slot where we can insert the samples to measure. - STM tip (2, pink): The STM tip is a chemically etched metallic rod clamped in a platform that magnetically attaches to the top of a piezoelectric tube for fine movement. We place this piezoelectric on a motorized table which allows a tip movement on the macroscopic scale. All the experiments of this thesis have been carried out with a gold tip.

seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.3 The vibration dumping levels
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.3 The vibration dumping levels

As mentioned before, the distance between the STM tip and the sample is of the order of nanometers and the tunnel current reacts exponentially to changes on it. For this reason, the tip-sample distance must remain as stable as possible and free from outside mechanical vibrations. Thus, we require a vibration dumping system that minimizes all these mechanical vibrations. In our system, the vibration isolation system has the following elements: - First, the entire experimental setup is on top of a foundation of concrete which is isolated from the rest of the building. This foundation minimizes the vibrations that come from the exterior of the institute and even outside our laboratory. - Secondly, the STM Chamber and Preparation Chamber are on top of a stainless-steel structure suspended by pneumatic legs from Newport [69].

seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.4 The Lock-in Amplifier
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.4 The Lock-in Amplifier

We use a lock-in amplifier to obtain experimentally the derivative of the tunnelling current with respect the voltage with a low noise-signal ratio. The lock-in amplifier employed in our experiments is a Stanford SR830. This instrument measures the amplitude and phase of an electrical oscillating signal. In our case, the lock-in amplifier measures the input signal that we want to measure plus a periodic reference signal used to probe the first one. Figure 3.5, depicts the schematic representation of the lock-in amplifier work processes. The reference signal $V_{ref}(\omega,\ t)$ described above is added to the bias voltage, so that it now contains DC and AC components. $$V_{bias}(t) = \ V_{bias,\ \ DC} + \ V_{mod}sin(\omega t)$$       (27) Where $V_{mod}\sin(\omega t) = V_{ref}(\omega,\ t)$ is both the AC component of the bias voltage and the reference signal that we feed to the lock-in amplifier, and $V_{bias,\ \ DC}$ corresponds to the DC component of the bias voltage.

Modulating the bias voltage makes that the tunnelling current also oscillates at the reference frequency, $I_{tunnel}(\omega,t)$. The time dependent tunnelling current that comes from the experiment is amplified by a factor G and converted into a voltage signal in the pre-amplifier according to the relation below. $$V_{sig}(t) = GI(t)$$                                             (29) Then, $V_{ref}$ passes through a phase shifter that shifts the phase in an angle $\alpha$ and both signals, $V_{sig}$ and the phase shifted $V_{ref}$, are fed to a multiplier circuit, yielding an output signal given by the expression: $$V_{sig} \times \ V_{ref}\  \simeq GI\left( V_{bias,DC} \right)V_{mod}\sin(\omega t) - \ G\frac{V_{mod}^{2}}{2}\cos(\alpha)\frac{dI\left( V_{bias,DC} \right)}{dV} + G\frac{V_{mod}^{2}}{2}\cos(2\omega t + \ \alpha)\frac{dI\left( V_{bias,DC} \right)}{dV}\ $$   (30) Finally, this product $V_{sig} \times \ V_{ref}$ goes through a low pass filter, usually with a cut-off frequency at $\omega/2$. The cut-off filter takes out all terms that present a frequency higher than $\omega/2$.

Finally, this product $V_{sig} \times \ V_{ref}$ goes through a low pass filter, usually with a cut-off frequency at $\omega/2$. The cut-off filter takes out all terms that present a frequency higher than $\omega/2$. The pre-amplified signals ($V_{sig}^{1}$, $V_{sig}^{2}$, $V_{sig}^{3}$) will present different areas according to the values of the modulated signal, and the slope of the I(V) curve in the region where the modulated signal falls. seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.5 Spectroscopy mapping: CITS
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.5 Spectroscopy mapping: CITS

For the investigations carried out in this thesis, the spatial extension of electronic states and quasiparticle excitations is very important. There are two main approaches to obtain spatial spectroscopic differences with STS, this is Continuous Imaging Tunnel Spectroscopy (CITS) and dI/dV maps. While ideally, they should yield the same results, the different conditions used for each of them makes them not completely equivalent. Thus, it is important to understand when we use one technique or the other. A CITS is an image in which, for every pixel, the tip stops to take an STS curve. This means that the x and y pixels and the $\frac{dI}{dV}(E)$ forms our 3D data matrix. This technique gives us a big amount of electronic information for each pixel of the area scanned. From this set of data, we can plot the dI/dV at any energy in the scanned area.

The counterpart of these measurements is that, as it takes an STS curve for every pixel in the image, the measurement of a CITS can last up to 20 hours or more. The expression below gives an estimated amount of time required for a CITS. $$t_{measurment} \backsimeq {N\ pixels}_{x} \times \ {M\ pixels}_{y} \times \ t_{sts\ curve}$$   (32) For a usual CITS of 30 second spectra, on an image of 64 x 64 pixels we have an estimated time of approximately 34 hours. Importantly, while recording the dI/dV curves at every pixel, the feedback loop is disconnected, to move from one pixel to the next one the feedback is connected again. Hence, for a given stabilization voltage, the tip-surface distance stays fixed.

Importantly, while recording the dI/dV curves at every pixel, the feedback loop is disconnected, to move from one pixel to the next one the feedback is connected again. Hence, for a given stabilization voltage, the tip-surface distance stays fixed. For this reason, changes in the electronic structure at energies below the stabilization voltage will have an impact on the tip-surface distance. Thus, in a CITS experiment, changes in peak intensities at a given energy can be attributed to two reasons. One, real changes in the intensity of the corresponding DOS peaks. And two, different tip-surface distances due to changes on the DOS at other energies.

seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.6 Spectroscopy mapping: dI/dV maps
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.4 The STM and its Chamber > 3.4.6 Spectroscopy mapping: dI/dV maps

In a dI/dV map, the dI/dV signal coming out of the lock-in amplifier is stored as a function of the spatial position of the tip while it scans the area at a given bias voltage. dI/dV maps are much faster to take than CITSs, usually of the order of minutes. However, the information obtained in dI/dV maps only maps the electronic states with an energy equal to the stabilization bias voltage. The counter part of measuring a dI/dV map is that the tip does not stop at every pixel to take de dI/dV information. The modulation signal is being received at the same time the tip is scanning. This increases the number of terms that change with respect time. If the tip finds a step of an island of molecules, it will retract changing the tip-sample distance. Thus, the time dependence of the tip is not only given by the modulation signal from the Lock-in Amplifier. It is also convoluted by the scanning speed of the tip moving along the surface.

Thus, the time dependence of the tip is not only given by the modulation signal from the Lock-in Amplifier. It is also convoluted by the scanning speed of the tip moving along the surface. When the scanned surface is relatively flat, this effect does not change the results dramatically, and one can interpret the image as the DOS map. However, if the surface is rough, for example, changes in the height of approximately 3-4 Å in between molecules the convolution is much more noticeable. Finally, we treat both CITS and dI/dV maps, along with the STM images, with the WSxM software [70].

We use the Preparation chamber to clean and grow the samples at UHV in a controlled way. Between the STM and the Preparation chamber there is a valve (1, red) that prevents the contamination of the STM chamber from residual gases present on the Preparation chamber. These residues can be Ar^+^ ions from sputtering, materials degassed from measuring filaments, from the annealing or the sublimation during depositions on the sample. It works by means of a quartz crystal membrane that vibrates at a certain frequency which we can precisely measure.

- The Quartz Microbalance (2, blue): This instrument allows to control the deposition rate of the materials sublimated towards the samples. It works by means of a quartz crystal membrane that vibrates at a certain frequency which we can precisely measure. When some material adsorbs on this quartz crystal, the mass of the membrane changes and so does the frequency of the crystal. By measuring the crystal oscillation frequency with time, we can control the level of coverage we deposit on the sample [71]. - The Electron beam evaporator with Flux Monitor (EFM evaporator) (3, pink) from FOCUS: we use this instrument to deposit organic molecules on the sample. The evaporator presents three glass crucibles with powders of molecules inside. We can heat the crucibles independently as each one presents a water-cooling system that prevents cross contamination from the non-heated crucibles. In this thesis, we used the EFM evaporator to deposit C~90~, PdTPP, FeClTPP, BPEA and BPEN [72].

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.5 The Preparation Chamber > 3.5.1 General principles of sample preparation

Before depositing any material, the single crystal needs to present clean, flat, and present wide terraces. We clean the samples by cycles of sputtering and annealing. The cleaning cycles start by sputtering the single crystal, usually for 10 minutes at an Argon atmosphere of 10^-6^ mbars. We sputter the sample by means of an Ion source from SPECS [75]. For this process we apply an electric field of 1.5 kV that ionize the Ar atoms and accelerate them before colliding with the single crystal surface, creating some current on the sample, in our case 14 $\mu$A. The collisions of the Ar ions with the surface eject the outer layers of material. Thus, leaving a clean surface, but at the expense of increasing its roughness. Figure 3.7 Photograph of the Preparation Chamber. In this chamber, we clean and grow the samples.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.5 The Preparation Chamber > 3.5.1 General principles of sample preparation

We anneal the single crystal by increasing the temperature of the sample by radiative heat transfer, usually for 10 minutes. We use a Pyrolytic-Boron-Nitride (PBN) heater by Scientia Omicron [77] located near the slot of the manipulator where we introduce de samples. This gives enough energy to the surface atoms to rearrange following the atom disposition of the deeper layers of the crystal but not enough to melt it or change its crystalline structure. After some cycles (usually three) of alternated sputtering and annealing processes, the sample is clean, and we can deposit materials on its surface. We deposit the organic molecules or other materials by sublimating them on the clean single crystal surface. To do that, we use evaporators that present crucibles in which we insert the materials we want to evaporate. Then, we heat the crucible until its temperature reaches the sublimation temperature of the material.

To do that, we use evaporators that present crucibles in which we insert the materials we want to evaporate. Then, we heat the crucible until its temperature reaches the sublimation temperature of the material. The sublimation of the material leads to a partial pressure of the molecules in the crucible volume. The crucible presents a hole for which the molecules in gas phase go through by effusion, creating a molecular beam. To deposit the molecules, we place the clean surface in front of this molecular beam, where a fraction of the emitted molecules sticks to the surface. We can precisely control the level of sublimation by means of the Quartz Microbalance previously mentioned.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.6 The Load-Lock Chamber

We use the Load-Lock chamber (2, orange) (see Figure 3.8) for quick transfer of samples and tips from atmospheric pressure into the vacuum part of the chamber. This Chamber has a pumping system that consist of a membrane pump (4, blue) MVP 040-2 and a turbomolecular pump (3, red) HiPace 300, both from PFEIFFER Vacuum. In a membrane pump, the membrane periodically flexes, which causes progressive increases and decreases of the pump chamber's volume. Then, there is a pair of non-return check valves placed such that the air does not reverse its flow towards the chamber [78]. Both pumps connect the same way as the scroll pump and turbomolecular pump in the Preparation chamber. We can reduce the pressure in the load-lock from ambient pressure to 10^-8^ mbar in 2 hours. For samples that come from ambient pressure or need cleaving there is no necessity of incorporating an ionic pump to reach the UHV. For the former, they then go through cleaning cycles in the Preparation chamber.

In a membrane pump, the membrane periodically flexes, which causes progressive increases and decreases of the pump chamber's volume. Then, there is a pair of non-return check valves placed such that the air does not reverse its flow towards the chamber [78]. Both pumps connect the same way as the scroll pump and turbomolecular pump in the Preparation chamber. We can reduce the pressure in the load-lock from ambient pressure to 10^-8^ mbar in 2 hours. For the former, they then go through cleaning cycles in the Preparation chamber.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.7 Optical Set-up > 3.7.1 Spectrometer

A spectrometer is an instrument that resolves the incoming light intensity into its different contributions corresponding to different wavelengths. The spectrometer employed to do the experiments was the Shamrock 500 spectrometer [79] depicted by Figure 3.11 a. Figure 3.11 b shows a schematic representation of the path followed by the light beam that comes from the entrance port of the spectrometer, which presents a slit (1, pink) that controls the area of the entrance where the light can pass through. Then, the light beam, reflects in one of the two collimated mirrors (2, red), which are standard Al + MgF~2~ coated mirrors. The reflected beam arrives to the turret which contains the different diffraction gratings (3, green). The turret of the Shamrock 500 spectrometer can hold up to three different gratings. The diffracted light is later reflected on another collimated mirror (4, red) that directs the light beam towards the EMCCD Camera.

ruta: 3.7.2 Electron Multiplying Charge Coupled Device Camera (EMCCD)
seccion: Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.7 Optical Set-up > 3.7.2 Electron Multiplying Charge Coupled Device Camera (EMCCD)
texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.7 Optical Set-up > 3.7.2 Electron Multiplying Charge Coupled Device Camera (EMCCD)

For the light detection we use a Newton Electron Multiplying Charge-Coupled-Device (EMCCD) from OXFORD INSTRUMENTS [80], located at the exit of the Spectrometer. An EMCCD is an image sensor that detects and quantifies single photon events without an image intensifier. We achieve this by incorporating an electron multiplying structure into the chip. Before going further in detail in the works of an EMCCD Camera we will explain the usual Charge-Couple-Device (CCD) Camera to later incorporate the differences that an EMCCD Camera presents with respect a usual one. Generally, a CCD Camera is a sensor that converts a light signal into an electrical one that can later be digitized. There are two main parts in a CCD Camera: the sensor or image section and the readout register. The image section is the photo-active area of the camera exposed to the incoming light beam. When the light beam interacts with this area, it creates electrical charges forming a charge pattern in the grid.

When the light beam interacts with this area, it creates electrical charges forming a charge pattern in the grid.

Apart from the electron multiplying gain, the signal can be amplified by a factor up to four at the amplifier output, before the charges enter the gain register. There are two main differences between the CCD Camera and the EMCCD. Traditional CCD Cameras present high sensitivity with readout noise levels lower than \<10e- [81], however, with the counterpart of a slow readout process. This comes from the CCD charge amplifier which needs to be as wide as possible. As the noise is proportional to the bandwidth of the amplifier, the higher the speed of the amplifiers the higher the noise. General CCD Cameras have relatively low bandwidths and a slow readout process. EMCCD cameras overcame this slow readout velocity by adding a charge amplifier (Multiplication register) before the Analog to Digital Converter (ADC). This amplification process comes from electron impact ionization which generates new electrons.

EMCCD cameras overcame this slow readout velocity by adding a charge amplifier (Multiplication register) before the Analog to Digital Converter (ADC). This amplification process comes from electron impact ionization which generates new electrons. As this happens before the ADC it reduces the signal to noise ratio and hence allows for high sensitivity and higher speed than the usual CCD Camera. The second difference comes from the signal area. The majority of EMCCD cameras present the so-called Frame-Transfer CCD structure. This structure presents two areas, one image section exposed to the light beam and, another one the same size, covered in an opaque mask usually made of aluminum that acts as storage area. Figure 3.12 a, shows a schematic representation of this storage area along with the readout register, multiplication register and readout ADC. The charge pattern created in the image section automatically shifts to the storage area, behind the mask region of the chip.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.8 Fabrication of STM Au Tips

To measure with an STM, we need a metallic tip which is atomically sharp. In this thesis, we recorded the whole STM measurements with Au tips. To obtain an atomically sharp tip, we employ a common technique called electrochemical etching. Figure 3.13 a shows a schematic representation of the setup required for the electrochemical etching process. In our case, we use an Au wire of 0.4 mm of diameter for the fabrication of the Au tips. First, we use a piece of the Au wire as the cathode. With a micrometer screw, we submerge the cathode in a HCl and ethanol solution such that the tip of the Au wire forms a meniscus due to the surface tension, which is approximately 2 mm. The solution corresponds to a certain volume of HCl at 37% of concentration diluted with the same volume of ethanol. Then, we submerge another piece of Au wire in the solution which acts as the anode. For the anode, the piece of Au wire submerges deeper than for the cathode.

We chose Au tips for the measurements of this thesis due to higher plasmonic response with respect the other tips such as W tips. Figure 3.13 b, shows an image of an Au tip taken with an optical microscope. As seen in this image, the apex of the tip presents some undulatory shape characteristic of the chemical etching. To clean the tip in UHV, we sputter it with Ar ions. We cannot anneal the tip with current flashes due to its high conductivity. For future works, we are planning to employ Ag tips as they reach as well a high plasmonic response and usually towards higher energies.

texto:
Chapter 3: Experimental Set-up > 3.9 Conclusions

In this chapter we have presented the instrumentation that was available for the realization of the experiments described in this thesis. In particular, the Photon STM systems allows for the in-situ sample preparation procedures to produce atomically clean and flat single crystal surfaces and to cover them with sub-monolayer amounts of different materials. Moreover, it allows for a topographic, spectroscopic and optical characterization of the sample with atomic resolution, due to the Low-Temperature Omicron STM combined with the optical setup. Furthermore, many groups in Spain are designing and building several other systems of this sort, demonstrating the interest of the scientific community on the results that this kind of systems can obtain.

texto:
Chapter 4: C~90~ on Ag(111) and Au(111) and NaCl/Ag(111)

C~90~ on Ag(111) and Au(111) and NaCl/Ag(111) In this Chapter, we describe the adsorption and electronic properties of the last incorporation to the carbon nanoform family (fullerenes, CNTs, graphene and nanographene), the so-called Fullertubes. The well-known previous allotropes have contributed extensively to the development of the fields of modern Nanoscience and Nanotechnology. Being Fullertubes a central CNT body capped by the hemifullerene moieties at its ends, we expect that this allotrope presents intermediate properties between CNTs and Fullerenes. As for the previous carbon allotropes, many of their properties come from their electronic structure. Thus, characterizing the energies and wavefunctions of fullertubes becomes essential to determine its potential and field of application. Here, we studied the crystalline structure, the energies and orbital wavefunctions of D~5h~(I)-C~90~ fullertubes, adsorbed on Ag(111), Au(111) and NaCl/Ag(111).

Chapter 4: C~90~ on Ag(111) and Au(111) and NaCl/Ag(111) > 4.1 Carbon nanostructures

In this Chapter we show the first experimental study on the adsorption and electronic structure of a new form of carbon nanoform named fullertubes [83][84][85][86]. So far, the properties of carbon nanostructures have led to many developments in the fields of modern Nanoscience and Nanotechnology [87][88]. As a recently added allotrope, fullertubes represent a promising line of research towards further progress in these fields. Carbon is a very versatile element, and its valence allows it to form a wide variety of allotropes. Some of them have been long known, such as diamond or graphite. However, researchers have found in the previous decades, a new set of carbon allotropes with at least one dimension in the nanometer or subnanometer regime. For example, graphene (Figure 4.1 a) [89], which corresponds to a one-atom thick, two-dimensional stable structure with a honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms.

However, researchers have found in the previous decades, a new set of carbon allotropes with at least one dimension in the nanometer or subnanometer regime. For example, graphene (Figure 4.1 a) [89], which corresponds to a one-atom thick, two-dimensional stable structure with a honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms. By limiting the extension of graphene in one in-plane direction, we obtain the so-called graphene nanoribbons, depicted in Figure 4.1 b [90]. Also, a honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms can fold around a given axis, leading to a cylindrical long (infinite) structure, the carbon nanotube (CNT), shown in Figure 4.1 c [89]. Last, when the arrangement of carbon atoms forms a closed, finite size structure they receive the name of Fullerenes (see Figure 4.1 d) [89]. Fullerenes, as mentioned before, present a closed structure constituted by single and double bonds forming rings of five and six carbon atoms.

By limiting the extension of graphene in one in-plane direction, we obtain the so-called graphene nanoribbons, depicted in Figure 4.1 b [90]. Also, a honeycomb lattice of carbon atoms can fold around a given axis, leading to a cylindrical long (infinite) structure, the carbon nanotube (CNT), shown in Figure 4.1 c [89]. Last, when the arrangement of carbon atoms forms a closed, finite size structure they receive the name of Fullerenes (see Figure 4.1 d) [89]. Fullerenes, as mentioned before, present a closed structure constituted by single and double bonds forming rings of five and six carbon atoms.

As some examples, this carbon structures can be used as scaffold for diverse microfabrication techniques [99], environmental monitoring due to their active surface and their ability to absorb gases [100] and energy dissipation in self-organized nanostructures under the influence of an electric field [92]. Our molecule of study, the isomer D~5h~(I)-C~90~ depicted in Figure 4.1 e, belongs to the family of carbon structures named fullertubes. These carbon allotropes consist of a CNT central body capped by two hemifullerene moieties at its edges [101]. Although in principle we can categorized D~5h~(I)-C~90~ as a fullerene due to its finite size, it also shares some structural properties with carbon nanotubes, which is why it receives its name. Such molecular form allows us to expect that its properties may be a combination of both, fullerenes, and CNTs. This expectation might be particularly relevant for their electronic properties.

Such molecular form allows us to expect that its properties may be a combination of both, fullerenes, and CNTs. This expectation might be particularly relevant for their electronic properties. Whereas Fullerenes present an electronic structure with well-defined energies and localized wavefunctions, CNTs, due to its infinite length, allow for delocalized electronic states and energy bands, for which Bloch functions describe them. An interesting question is thus how the electronic structure of infinite CNTs become discretized as their length becomes shorter. In this scenario, the investigation of the energies and wavefunctions of fullertubes and its comparison with that of CNTs might help addressing the abovementioned question.

An interesting question is thus how the electronic structure of infinite CNTs become discretized as their length becomes shorter. In this scenario, the investigation of the energies and wavefunctions of fullertubes and its comparison with that of CNTs might help addressing the abovementioned question. For all the reasons described so far, our experiments focus on the study of the crystalline and electronic structures of the isomer D~5h~(I)-C~90~ adsorbed on the noble metal surfaces Au(111) and Ag(111) and on ultra-thin layers of the dielectric material NaCl over an Ag(111) surface. Placing a dielectric material in between the molecules and the metallic surface should lead to a more electronically decoupled molecule from the surface. Thus, we can expect their electronic structure to be more similar to the one corresponding to the gas phase than upon adsorption on metals.

We sublimated the C~90~ molecules from the evaporator at a temperature of 480 °C for 3 hours. We required such long deposition time due to the sublimation temperature which is close to the temperature of thermal decomposition. Therefore, we minimized the evaporation temperature to avoid the possible presence of chemically different molecules. Figure 4.2 b, depicts a STM image of the surface following deposition of C~90~ molecules. The molecules self-assemble into relatively large and well-ordered islands, showing step edges in three different directions forming an angle in between edges of approximately 113.0 $\pm$ 2.6° and 133.5 $\pm$ 1.0°. Individual molecules are imaged as elongated protrusions, with a long axis of 1.3 $\pm$ 0.04 nm and a short axis of 0.9 $\pm$ 0.04 nm, in good agreement with the expected length and diameter of the C~90~ molecules (see Figure 4.2 a). This analysis demonstrates a side-on adsorption configuration of the C~90~ molecules on the Au(111) surface.

The profile reveals a value of approximately 0.4 nm, approximately the vdW diameter of the molecule [102]. The black star represents the High Symmetry Directions of Au(111). STM image parameters: $I_{t} = 30.0\ pA$; $V_{bias} = 2.0\ V$ and $Size =$ 27.3 x 27.3 ${nm}^{2}$.

**Figure 4.4 Optimized equilibrium geometry of C~90~ molecules adsorbed in the Au(111) metallic surface.** The minimum energy corresponding to the adsorption geometry is more stable than the other structures by at least 0.3 eV, with an axial angle of 12° and a sample-molecule distance of 2.88 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$. This suggests an interaction of the molecule with the surfaces by vdW forces.

Figure 4.2 c, presents the height profile of the C~90~ island shown in Figure 4.2 b, which reveals a value of 0.4 nm for the apparent molecular height. Although the measured molecular height is smaller than the short molecular length, we believe that this effect can be due to electronic factors. For a decoupled molecule, we would expect the same value of both parameters as it should corresponds to its vdW diameter [102]. It also depicts the unit cell vectors of the C~90~ molecules (b~1~, b~2~) and the atomic lattice vectors of Au(111) (a~1~, a~2~) as blue and red arrows, respectively. The transformation matrix between both sets of lattice vectors follow approximately an integer relation. In the STM image of Figure 4.3 a, there seems to be a pattern of alternating brighter and darker rows. We can interpret it as a Moiré pattern coming from the small mismatch from the transformation matrix between (b~1~, b~2~) and (a~1~, a~2~). However, this bright and dark pattern does not follow through the whole area of the island. It seems that the defects on the island's surface give these structures at a long-range order. For surfaces with low density of defects this structure tends to disappear. All these observations suggest that van der Waals (vdW) interactions control both, the adsorption of the molecules on the metal and the assembly of the molecules into closed-packed structures.

For surfaces with low density of defects this structure tends to disappear. All these observations suggest that van der Waals (vdW) interactions control both, the adsorption of the molecules on the metal and the assembly of the molecules into closed-packed structures. Taking into consideration only intermolecular interactions, vdW forces would tend to aggregate the molecules in a 2D arrangement with the long molecular axis in an out-of-plane direction, since the packing would be closer in this geometry. The observation that the molecular axis orients in-plane demonstrates that, for the adsorption of C~90~ molecules on the Au(111) surface, molecule-substrate interactions dominate over molecule-molecule interactions. Also, and as we will discuss below, this adsorption geometry is ideal for the investigation of the longitudinal spatial distribution of the molecular orbitals, which is important to compare it with the bands in the corresponding [5,5]-CNT.

In Figure 4.4, we show the calculated optimized geometry of the C~90~ molecules on the metallic surface. The relatively large bonding distances obtained, 2.88 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$, indicate an interaction between the molecules and the surface predominantly by vdW, as mentioned above. Also, the minimum energy adsorption configuration shows that the long molecular axis orients parallel to the surface plane and aligns with the closed packed direction of Au(111), in good agreement with our experimental observations. Also, the theoretical analysis has revealed many relaxed structures with different axial angles. As shown in Figure 4.4, we defined the axial angle as the angle between the substrate's surface plane and the one formed by the long axis of the molecule and the carbon-carbon bond from the upper pentagon of the hemifullerene moiety. Between these structures, the more stable geometry is the one depicted in the image, with an axial angle of $12^{o}$.

We prepared the sample following a similar procedure as for the previous metallic surface. We sublimated C~90~ on Ag(111) at the same temperature as on Au(111) but exposing it for a shorter time of 2 hours to Ag(111). After that, we did a post-annealing of 100 °C and 10 minutes. Figure 4.5 a, shows that as it is the most reactive area, most nucleation points will be at the steps of the Ag(111) terraces and from there, the islands will grow. From this figure, we also observe the nucleation of a second layer of molecules on top of the islands near the terraces of Ag(111). Measuring a smaller area, we find in Figure 4.5 b, a topographic image of the molecular arrangement of C~90~ molecules within the islands. Once again, the molecules are imaged as elongated protrusions, with a long axis of 1.3 $\pm$ 0.04 nm and a short axis of 0.9 $\pm$ 0.02 nm. Both, in good agreement with the expected length and diameter of the C~90~ molecules (see Figure 4.5 d).

In the previous sections we found that depositing the molecules directly over the metallic surface, molecule-surface interaction plays a role in the assembly of the islands, which might also potentially affect their electronic structure. One possible way to solve this difficulty would be to use an insulating thin film to decouple the molecules. To explore this idea, we placed a dielectric material (NaCl) in between the molecules of study and the metallic surface. We prepared the sample by heating the crucible of the evaporator containing NaCl at 470 °C and exposing it for 1 hour over a clean surface of Ag(111) at approximately 100 °C. After the thermalization of the sample, we sublimated the C~90~ molecules heating its crucible at 480 °C and exposing it to the substrate for 3 hours. Figure 4.9 c presents a topography image of the obtained sample~,~ where different regions can be identified as Ag(111), 2-3 ML NaCl/Ag(111) and C~90~ islands on top of the NaCl films.

To obtain information about the molecular orbitals of C~90~ molecules, we have recorded dI/dV spectra at different positions of the molecular lattice (see Figure 4.11 a). Figure 4.11 b shows these positions by crosses of different colors. One at the intersection of three molecules (yellow), another at the intersection of two molecules (green) and the last ones at the hemifullerene moieties (red and blue). The dI/dV curves show that the intensity ratios of the different peaks, and, to some extent, their energy positions depend on the location where we recorded the spectra. However, we can observe some general trends in all spectra. At negative voltages, we find a conductance step at approximately -1.20 V on the four curves that can be interpreted as the HOMO level of the molecules. For positive voltages, we find peaks at 0.70 V, 0.84 V and 1.75 V, that we in principle attribute to the LUMO, LUMO+1 and LUMO+2 orbitals.

The spectral features in the dI/dV have a very important role on the voltage dependence of the STM images. Figure 4.12 a to d, depicts topography images of C~90~ molecules over the Au(111) metallic surface at different voltages, -1.35, 0.63, 0.84, and 1.7 V, respectively, corresponding to the voltages at which we can identify the spectral features in Figure 4.11. Due to the molecular gap, the images recorded at -1.35 eV and 0.63 eV must correspond to the spatial extension of the HOMO and LUMO, respectively. To discriminate between the effect of the metal substrate and the electronic structure of the molecules in gas phase, we also gathered information about the MOs of the C~90~ molecules on Ag(111). These locations correspond to one at the center of the molecule (blue), the edge of the molecule (red) and between two molecules (green) with the exact location of the curves presented in Figure 4.13 b.
