For a better identification of the MO of the C~90~ molecules we compared the results on both metals. Figure 4.15 depicts the mean dI/dV curves from a CITS averaged over a molecule of C~90~ on Ag(111) (grey) and Au(111) (yellow). As previously discussed, below the Fermi level at negative voltages, the location of the step that we can attribute to the HOMO level has similar value in energy on both substrates. However, for the LUMO, LUMO+1 and LUMO+2, they present a difference in energy of approximately 0.6 V. The electronic gap between both metals is different. The gap for Ag(111) is lower than the one of Au(111). This might be due to a different screening that related the electron-electron repulsion due to a bigger charge transfer on Ag(111) than on Au(111) as previously described for C~60~ on Ag and Au surfaces [104][105]. c) 700.0 pA; 1.1 V. d) 1.5 nA; 1.7 V Having experimentally confirmed the expected shape of the MOs of C~90~ molecules, now we will discuss the relation with the electronic states in carbon nanotubes. Here, we will stablish a comparison between the spatial extension of the frontier orbitals of our molecule and the delocalized (Bloch) states characteristic of the infinite [5,5]-SWCNT. Bloch wave functions $e^{ikx}u(\mathbf{r})$ define the delocalized electronic states in a CNT, where $u(\mathbf{r})$ is a function with the periodicity of the lattice that represents the spatial extension of the electronic states for $k = 0$ ($\Gamma$ point). A given wave function for a non-vanishing value of $k$ within the same band is the product of $u(\mathbf{r})$ and a one-dimensional (1D) harmonic wave. For a nanotube of finite length $L$, due to quantum confinement, the electron momentum's ($k_{n\ }'s$) values would be discrete and given by $k_{n\ } = \ \frac{n\pi}{L}$ being n, an integer value.

A given wave function for a non-vanishing value of $k$ within the same band is the product of $u(\mathbf{r})$ and a one-dimensional (1D) harmonic wave. For a nanotube of finite length $L$, due to quantum confinement, the electron momentum's ($k_{n\ }'s$) values would be discrete and given by $k_{n\ } = \ \frac{n\pi}{L}$ being n, an integer value. With all this, the wave function of such an electronic state corresponds to the product of $u(\mathbf{r})$ and a sinusoidal standing wave with $n - 1$ nodes. Figure 4.18 a and c, show a comparison between the wave functions of the HOMO and LUMO+2 orbitals of the C~90~ molecule with respect the wavefunction of the CNT for the Valence Band. Both figures depict how we can define the orbitals of the fullertube of length $L$ as the result of the quantum confinement of an infinite CNT, with $n = 2$ and $n = 3$, respectively. The strong confinement of the molecular orbitals in the fullertube leads to nodes at both hemifullerene terminals.

As for the LUMO+1 orbital, the dependence with the polar angle does not present similarities with the bands of [5,5]-SWCNT. Figure 4.17 b, shows as non-vanishing value of the wave function at the hemifullerene moieties. Also, its molecular orbital, defined by a nodal plane containing the long axis of the molecule, does not present rotational symmetry such as the 5-fold symmetry of the CNT moiety. This suggests that, on one hand, when the orbitals with azimuthal dependence are compatible with such CNTs 5-fold symmetry, we can define them as the delocalized bands discretized due to quantum confinement. And, on the other hand, when fullertubes present electronic states that do not match with such 5-fold symmetry, they correspond to a fullerene-like state. While the dependence of the STM images with bias voltage does not show such a rich variety of structures, because we only have access to the hemifullerene endcap, we can still observe some interesting. For example, Figure 4.20 presents two topography images at different bias voltages of the C~90~ molecules on a dielectric layer of NaCl on top of Ag(111). Figure 4.20 b, shows the topography image of the molecules at 1.2 V where the MO present a triangular shape. As shown in the section 4.2.3, the molecules in this surface assemble with its long axis perpendicular to the surface.

Chapter 4: C~90~ on Ag(111) and Au(111) and NaCl/Ag(111) > 4.6 Conclusions

To conclude, we have for the first time studied the structural and electronic properties of C~90~ molecules by means of STM imaging and spectroscopy. STM images of the islands of C~90~ on both metallic surfaces, Ag(111) and Au(111) show a rhomboidal self-assembly of the molecules with the long axis of the molecules parallel to the surface. Thus, the molecule-substrate interaction is stronger than the molecule-molecule interaction having an adsorption behavior similar to fullerene molecules. The resolution of the STM images allows us to create some lattice models for the molecules on both metallic surfaces. In the case of C~90~/Ag(111), the lattice vectors of the islands of C~90~ follow an integer relation with respect the lattice vectors of the Ag(111) surface. For the C~90~/Au(111) experiments, the relation between the lattice vector of the C~90~ molecule's island and the Au(111) surface follows approximately the same integer relation as the previous metal.

The dI/dV curves taken at different locations of the C~90~ molecules for the two metallic surfaces allowed us to obtain the energies and shapes of MOs observed on the dI/dV maps. These spectra reveal the position of the HOMO, LUMO and some higher unoccupied states at larger voltages. By comparing the mean dI/dV curve averaged over the surface of the C~90~ islands on both Au(111) and Ag(111), we can determine that the HOMO level does not present a shift in energy whereas the LUMO level and the rest of the unoccupied states observed present a shift with respect both metallic surfaces of approximately 0.6 V. This difference corresponds to the difference between the work functions of Au(111) and Ag(111) [106]. Density Functional Theory calculations along with our experimental results, revealed that we can classify the electronic states of the fullertubes according to their resemblance with the electronic structure of the infinite [5,5]-SWCNT.

This difference corresponds to the difference between the work functions of Au(111) and Ag(111) [106]. Density Functional Theory calculations along with our experimental results, revealed that we can classify the electronic states of the fullertubes according to their resemblance with the electronic structure of the infinite [5,5]-SWCNT. Some fullertube orbitals can be defined as the discretized version of the delocalized Bloch states of the infinite CNT band due to strong quantum confinement, suggesting a nanotube-like electronic structure. However, other fullertube orbitals are more localized at its edges indicating an origin unrelated to quantum confinement of infinite CNT bands which suggest a fullerene-like electronic structure. Finally, we have developed some diverse recipes for the fabrication of C~90~ nanostructures and studied their crystalline and electronic structures on different substrates.

Chapter 5: Effects of the Adsorption on Single Molecules on the Plasmonic modes of the STM Nanocavity

Effects of the Adsorption on Single Molecules on the Plasmonic modes of the STM Nanocavity As discussed in chapter 2, researchers are currently exploiting STM techniques to study the optical properties of different materials. From metallic surfaces to organic molecules insulated from the metal by a thin dielectric film. So far, the quenching of luminescence described in Chapter 2 did not allow to study the optical properties of molecules directly adsorbed on metal surfaces by STM. In this Chapter, we explore an alternative route, based on the characterization of the effects of the adsorption of individual organic molecules on the plasmonic modes of the nanocavity formed between the tip and the sample of an STM. After an introduction to the topic in general and to the molecules that we investigated (BPEA and BPEN), we will describe the morphology of BPEA and BPEN molecules adsorbed on Au(111) and Ag(111).

After an introduction to the topic in general and to the molecules that we investigated (BPEA and BPEN), we will describe the morphology of BPEA and BPEN molecules adsorbed on Au(111) and Ag(111). We continue with a discussion about their electronic properties, being able to locate in energy their HOMO and LUMO levels through dI/dV curves and CITSs. We will also determine their shape through spatially resolved dI/dV maps of both molecules BPEA and BPEN on both metallic surfaces (Au(111) and Ag(111)). At this point, we studied the optical properties of the plasmonic tunnel junctions including these molecules on Au(111).

We will also determine their shape through spatially resolved dI/dV maps of both molecules BPEA and BPEN on both metallic surfaces (Au(111) and Ag(111)). At this point, we studied the optical properties of the plasmonic tunnel junctions including these molecules on Au(111). For this purpose, we acquire raw electroluminescence spectra on both molecules and the metal and immediately after every spectrum, a I(V) curve. With this information we were able to apply the normalization procedure, separating the effects of the electronic structure of the system from the Optical Radiative Density also known as the Purcell factor. As we will show later in the chapter, while the raw spectra of empty and molecule-filled cavities are very different, the normalization procedure largely removes these effects. However, we must attribute the remaining differences to changes in the cavity plasmon modes due to the presence of the molecule.

As we will show later in the chapter, while the raw spectra of empty and molecule-filled cavities are very different, the normalization procedure largely removes these effects. However, we must attribute the remaining differences to changes in the cavity plasmon modes due to the presence of the molecule. These differences also, must be related to differences in the frequency dependent on the dielectric constant and, thus, to the optical properties of the system metal-molecule. Finally, we compared our experimental results to a theoretical model that includes the coupling between the inelastic transition dipole moment of tunnel electrons and the dipole moments of the molecular optical transitions. This is a sort of absorption experiment in which the cavity plasmons excited by inelastic electrons replace the probe light beam.

Previously STML has proven to allow the study of the optical properties of organic molecules enclosed within plasmonic nanojunctions. However, until now researchers carried out experiments with a dielectric layer insulating the molecules from the metal surface. In this case, the electroluminescence spectra recorded with the tip placed on top of the molecule show features corresponding to the excitonic states of the molecule [107][108][109][110]. The organic molecules must be electronically decoupled from the Chapter 5: Effects of Adsorption on Single Molecules on Plasmonic modes of an STM Nanocavity metallic substrate by atomic layers of a dielectric material, usually NaCl [107]. The dielectric prevents the energy transfer to the metal and hence, optical quenching. When the molecules are in direct contact with a metal surface, the optical quenching process is much faster than the radiative recombination of the excitons and prevents molecular emission.

The dielectric prevents the energy transfer to the metal and hence, optical quenching. When the molecules are in direct contact with a metal surface, the optical quenching process is much faster than the radiative recombination of the excitons and prevents molecular emission. The necessity of a dielectric material such as NaCl, strongly restricts the kind of molecules that STML can address to study its optical properties. The presence of a dielectric layer reduces molecule-substrate interaction and not every molecule can remain fixed on top of these layers. Moreover, in some cases the interest relays on studying the optical properties of molecules synthesized directly on the metal surface [111]. This interest calls for new methods to obtain this optical information. On the other hand, the presence of organic molecules on plasmonic cavities should lead to measurable differences in their plasmonic modes as previously introduced in Chapter 2.

This interest calls for new methods to obtain this optical information. On the other hand, the presence of organic molecules on plasmonic cavities should lead to measurable differences in their plasmonic modes as previously introduced in Chapter 2. For example, these differences in the plasmonic modes allows for the fabrication of nano-sensors as the one described in reference [26] and discussed in the mentioned chapter. Moreover, organic molecules embedded in plasmonic junctions can lead to Rabi splitting once reached the strong light-matter coupling regime. This phenomenon, also discussed in Chapter 2, offers great interest at a single molecule level which requires atomic-scale spatial resolution. Thus, the picometer resolution of the STM represents a great tool for studying these effects on the plasmonic modes.

This phenomenon, also discussed in Chapter 2, offers great interest at a single molecule level which requires atomic-scale spatial resolution. Thus, the picometer resolution of the STM represents a great tool for studying these effects on the plasmonic modes. Due to the previous discussion, we expect that the modifications of the plasmonic emission of an individual molecule in direct contact with the metallic surface give optical information of the molecule in the STM junction. Also, the STM technique would give us the opportunity to measure these changes in the plasmonic modes with atomic-scale spatial resolution. However, previous attempts at obtaining information about the cavity plasmons in the presence of organic molecules have not found clear trends. In Figure 5.1, we show the changes in the raw STM luminescence spectra due to the presence of adsorbed organic molecules, for two different works in the literature, [112] and [113].

However, previous attempts at obtaining information about the cavity plasmons in the presence of organic molecules have not found clear trends. In Figure 5.1, we show the changes in the raw STM luminescence spectra due to the presence of adsorbed organic molecules, for two different works in the literature, [112] and [113]. In [112], the sample studied was hexa-*tert*-butyl-decacyclene (HBDC), (shown in Figure 5.1 a) sublimated on a Cu(111) surface as shown in Figure 5.1 b. In the photon map of Figure 5.1 c, the light intensity recorded with the tip placed on top of the molecules is significantly larger that when the tip is over the bare metal surface. Attending to Figure 5.1 d, the light emission on the molecule doubles the one of Cu(111). Moreover, and although it is relatively subtle, the plasmonic response presents a blue shift in energy with respect the metal with the peak wavelength separated by around 4 nm [14].

For this work we have chosen two organic molecules as the quantum emitters, 9,10-bis(phenylethynyl)anthracene or BPEA (see Figure 5.3 a), and 5,12-bis(phenylethynyl)naphthalene or BPEN (see Figure 5.3 b). Both, look very similar in its structure except for the polyaromatic body, being anthracene for the BPEA and naphthalene for the BPEN. However, they present significant differences on their absorption spectra. Figure 5.3 c shows both absorption spectra for BPEA and BPEN in toluene solution measured with standard absorption spectroscopy. The absorption spectrum for BPEN (orange curve) presents its peak at 2.2 eV. The energy range in which the optical transitions of BPEN take place, thus, is very similar to the energy range of the plasmonic emission from empty cavities formed between gold STM tips and noble metal surfaces. For the absorption curve of BPEA (cyan curve), the peak locates at around 2.7 eV, which is 0.5 eV higher in energy with respect BPEN [114].

The electronic properties of the molecules can give us information about the energy levels and molecular orbitals of quantum emitters which will be necessary to clarify their role in the measured light emission. For these reasons we now present an electronic characterization of adsorbed BPEA and BPEN molecules. For BPEA on the Ag(111) surface we show, in Figure 5.8 a, the mean dI/dV curve averaged over a region of the organic molecule from a CITS (black curve). For positive voltages, at 0.6 V there is a peak (vertical dashed line) that can be interpreted as the LUMO level of the molecule as it does not appear in the dI/dV curve averaged over a region of Ag(111) (orange curve). Figure 5.8 b, presents the dI/dV map recorded at 0.6 V which is the bias voltage corresponding to the LUMO level of the BPEA. This orbital shows three relatively dim lobes at the phenyl terminals, and two bright lobes at the anthracene ends.

Figure 5.8 b, presents the dI/dV map recorded at 0.6 V which is the bias voltage corresponding to the LUMO level of the BPEA. This orbital shows three relatively dim lobes at the phenyl terminals, and two bright lobes at the anthracene ends. At negative voltages, the curve in Figure 5.8 a does not seem to show a defined peak. Thus, we cannot identify the position in energy of the HOMO level of the molecule. This may be because the HOMO level is lower in energy than the range measured in the dI/dV curve. As, due to excitonic effects, the optical gap is usually lower than the electronic one. Based on the absorption spectra of Figure 5.3 c, we expect the HOMO level to appear at energies lower than 2.7 V below the LUMO level, this means below -2.1 V. As the reactivity of Ag(111) is different than the previous metal, the sticking coefficient of the molecules to the surface is also different. For the desired molecular density, we followed the same procedure as the previous metal but slightly changed some parameters. We heated the evaporator at 170°C for both molecules, exposing the single crystal of Au(111) on the manipulator at RT to a flux of sublimated molecules of 20 seconds for each one. Figure 5.10 a shows an STM topographic image of both BPEA and BPEN on Au(111). As in the previous metal they do not self-assemble. However, there is a clear patterning effect from the underlying herringbone reconstruction. Most molecules adsorb either at the elbows of the reconstruction or in the FCC areas. The spatial resolution of the STM allows us to distinguish between both BPEA and BPEN on the same image, see Figure 5.10 b. Figure 5.10 c depicts a stick and ball models for both molecules with the same orientation as the previous image.

Interestingly, we can also observe a new broad resonance for the molecules on Au(111) around the Fermi level. While we can also identify a similar structure in the spectra recorded on top of the BPEA molecules (curves 3 and 4), the intensity of the resonance is lower. We present the spatial distribution of such state in Figure 5.15 a, showing a CITS cut at 6 mV. The intensity of the dI/dV curves at this energy decreases when the tip locates on top of the BPEA molecules, disappearing at the anthracene longitudinal edges. More importantly, by changing the contrast of the image to exclude this dimmer area of the molecule, we observe a bright fringe surrounding the molecule, see Figure 5.15 b. Thus, we believe that contrary to the previous metal, on Au(111) a new state appears due to the absorption of the molecule.

To investigate the role of BPEA and BPEN molecules on the plasmonic modes of the cavity, we have grown a sample in which both molecules have been co-deposited on Au(111), like that of Figure 5.10. Figure 5.18 a shows the raw light emission obtained on the Au(111) surface and on top of both BPEA and BPEN molecules, depicted in black, red, and blue, respectively. Although they look similar in shape, there is a significant decrease of the raw intensity on the spectra obtained for the molecules with respect the metal. Obtaining lower light intensity on the molecules with respect the metal is usually the case reported in previous studies and is in line with our observations for different molecules [113]. However, other reports have found a larger intensity on the adsorbed molecules [112].

Chapter 5: Effects of the Adsorption on Single Molecules on the Plasmonic modes of the STM Nanocavity > 5.5 Optical effects of BPEA and BPEN on LSPR between an Au STM tip and an Au(111) surface > 5.5.1 Raw vs. Normalized spectra

Obtaining lower light intensity on the molecules with respect the metal is usually the case reported in previous studies and is in line with our observations for different molecules [113]. However, other reports have found a larger intensity on the adsorbed molecules [112]. As described in the introduction to this chapter (Section 5.1), we want to explore if these changes arise from true differences in the optical response of the cavities due to the presence of the molecules, or from a different electronic factor. Following the normalization procedure described above, we estimated the electronic factor (dashed lines in Figure 5.18 a) from the I(V) curves recorded together with the raw luminescence spectra (continuous lines in Figure 5.18 a). Then we divided the luminescence spectra by the electronic factor, yielding the normalized spectra of Figure 5.18 b [113].

Although the shapes of the normalized spectra look very similar to one another, there are still some minor differences. First, Figure 5.19 a, shows a shift in the energy peak with respect the metallic response by about 10 meV. We believe that this shift might be due to the slightly larger cavity arising from the tip retraction when it moves to the top of the molecule. The retraction of the tip is a consequence of keeping constant the current applied. Figure 5.19 b, depicts the height profile of the molecule, and we can observe that the tip retracts approximately 1.5 Å when it scans across the molecule. Theoretical calculations of the plasmon energies predict a shift in energy of 4 to 10 meV/Å [51] (see Figure 5.19 c), when the distance between the tip and the metal surface is different. This means that our experimental 10 meV shift in energy is in good agreement with the one expected from a retraction of 1.5 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$.

In our experiments we can identify different elements that our model should include. First, we have a plasmonic cavity that corresponds to the gap between the tip and sample. The inelastic tunneling electrons excite the plasmonic modes. Upon an inelastic transition, an electron from an initial energy level E~i~ in one electrode transfers to a final state of energy E~f~ located at the other electrode. Such transfer has associated a transition dipole moment which oscillates in time with a frequency given by the energy difference between E~i~ and E~f~. We can thus model the inelastic excitation as arising from a first dipole moment that excites plasmonic modes. Such excited plasmon modes can now interact with the adsorbed molecules, possibly inducing molecular excitations, which we can also describe by a transition dipole moment. In summary, we need to explain the interaction between a first and a second dipole momenta.

Such excited plasmon modes can now interact with the adsorbed molecules, possibly inducing molecular excitations, which we can also describe by a transition dipole moment. In summary, we need to explain the interaction between a first and a second dipole momenta. The first corresponding to the inelastic tunnel transition and a the second one to the molecular excitation, mediated by the cavity plasmons. Reference [116] carries out such a theoretical study of two quantum emitters (QEs) that interact via a plasmonic junction. Figure 5.22 a shows a schematic representation of this model. To compare such theory to our experimental situation, we interpret the first QE of dipole moment $\mu$ (red), as corresponding to the inelastic tunnelling transitions. The second QE of dipole moment $\mu_{E}$ (blue), represents the optical transition associated to the organic molecule placed in the nanocavity. The existence of $\mu_{E}$ perturbs the plasmonic modes of the cavity.

From our previous analysis we believe to have identified an optical transition within both BPEA and BPEN molecules on Au(111). However, it is difficult to attribute such transition to HOMO-LUMO excitations such as the ones observed by optical spectroscopy. One reason is that the optical gaps of the molecules in solution is larger than the observed 1.68 eV and, moreover, is different for both molecules. Also, due to the planar shape of the molecules, the orientation of the transition dipole moments associated to HOMO-LUMO excitations are parallel to the molecular plane. However, we expect the electric field associated to the cavity plasmons to be perpendicular to such direction. All these observations arise the following question. What is the nature of the optical transition corresponding to the step in the $\mathrm{\Delta}P/P$ curves at 1.68 eV. As tentative answers to the last question, we consider two possible explanations.

To conclude, the electronic factors play an important role in the light intensity changes of the raw spectra, being largely a consequence of them. The necessity to measure at constant current causes a blue shift on the normalized spectra with respect the metallic surface as a change in the distance between the tip and the sample. Finally, by attending to the changes of the spectral distribution of the normalized intensities we can study the optical properties of individual organic molecules on direct metallic surfaces. Notice that we could not extract optical information from individual molecules on metals by direct excitation of molecular luminescence due to the quenching effect of the metal [24]. However, as there is a coupling between the excitonic modes of the molecules and the plasmonic modes of the metal, by studying the changes on these plasmonic modes caused by the molecule, we can study the optical properties of the very same molecule.

Chapter 6: Adsorption and emission effects of PdTPP and FeClTPP on noble metal surfaces

Adsorption and emission effects of PdTPP and FeClTPP on noble metal surfaces In Chapter 5 we found that the adsorption of organic molecules on metal surfaces can affect their plasmonic response. This adsorption causes the formation of hybrid molecule-metal electronic states which can be involved in the optical transitions of the surface. The purpose of this Chapter 6 is to explore the changes in the plasmonic emission by molecules where the optical transitions come from molecular orbitals of the molecule. These transitions are HOMO-LUMO instead of metal-molecule transitions. To study these transitions, we will measure the plasmonic electroluminescence spectra of a different set of molecules. We chose them regarding three important structural features. Firstly, their optical transitions involve molecular orbitals localized in planar polyaromatic areas. Secondly, they have bulky groups at the periphery of the polyaromatic areas.

Thus, the optical transitions will have dipole momenta with out-of-plane components.

For the following experiments we chose two organic molecules with similar structure, palladium(II) meso-tetraphenylporphine or PdTPP and meso-tetraphenylporphine chloride or FeClTPP (Figure 6.1 a and Figure 6.1 b, respectively). Both PdTPP and FeClTPP molecules present four phenyl groups that, in the gas-phase configuration, are tilted with respect the plane of the molecule, see Figure 6.1 c and Figure 6.1 d, respectively. We expect that this tilt in the phenyl groups allow them to act as legs that separate the body of the molecule with respect the metallic surface, thus, making it difficult for the substrate-molecule transitions to occur. The difference between these two organic molecules is not only the metal atom. Also, the FeClTPP presents a Cl atom attached to the Fe atom at the center of the porphine. Due to this Cl atom, FeClTPP may present a dipole moment perpendicular to the surface.

We sublimated PdTPP by heating the evaporator at 260 $_°C$, exposing the Au(111) single crystal surface to the molecular beam for 1 minute. The monocrystal remained in the manipulator of the Preparation Chamber at Room Temperature (RT) during the deposition. Figure 6.3 a, shows an STM image recorded at 4.7 K of the Au(111) surface after the sublimation of the molecules. As shown in the figure, they do tend to self-assemble forming square islands of different sizes (Figure 6.3 a). Moreover, one of the two directions of the edges of the islands follows the HSDs of Au(111). Figure 6.3 b shows an island with a size of approximately 3 x 5 nm. The resolution of the STM allow us to distinguish the number of molecules on each island as the one in Figure 6.3 b. This island presents an area of 3 x 4 PdTPP molecules lacking the last one at the top-right side.

To sublimate the FeClTPP molecules on Au(111) we employed the same procedure than with the previous molecules. We heated the evaporator at 260 $_°C$ exposing the single crystal of Au(111) to a flux of sublimated molecules for 1 minute. The single crystal was in the manipulator of the preparation chamber and kept at RT during the deposition. Figure 6.7 a, shows a large scale STM image of the FeClTPP molecules on Au(111). As with the previous molecules, the FeClTPP tends to self-assemble into well-ordered squared islands, although the average island size is larger. Also, one of the two directions of the edges of the FeClTPP islands follows the HSDs of Au(111). Figure 6.7 b, depicts an STM image taken on the surface of the island where we can distinguish individual molecules. Some molecules on the surface appear dimmer than others. As a tentative answer to this different brightness, we propose that during the sublimation or adsorption process, some molecules lose the Cl axial ligand.

We sublimated the PdTPP molecule by heating the evaporator at 260 °C and exposing the Ag(111) single crystal surface to the molecular flux for 3 minutes. The single crystal remained in the manipulator of the preparation chamber at RT. Figure 6.11 a, shows an STM image of the Ag(111) surface with the PdTPP molecules sublimated on top. In this large-scale image, we observe that the molecules tend to self-assemble forming big terraces and not a variety of different sizes of islands as in Au(111). As a tentative explanation for this observation, we believe that the elbows at the herringbone of the previous metal act as nucleation points. In the case of Ag(111), the terraces edges act as nucleation points leading to the formation of these big terraces. Moreover, the directions of the edges of such big terraces do not tend to follow the HSD of Ag(111). Figure 6.11 b, depicts an STM image the frontier of one of the big islands from Figure 6.11 a.

For the sublimation of FeClTPP molecules on Ag(111) we followed the same procedure as for the previous molecule. We heated the evaporator at 260 °C and exposed the single crystal of Ag(111) to the molecular flux for 3 minutes. During the deposition, the single crystal of Ag(111) was also in the manipulator of the preparation chamber at RT. Figure 6.15 a, shows a large-scale STM image of the FeClTPP molecules on Ag(111). As with the previous molecules, the FeClTPP also tends to self-assemble into terraces. This is because the edges of the terraces of Ag(111) are the main source of the nucleation points. Furthermore, also the directions of the terrace do not tend to follow the HSDs of Ag(111). Figure 6.15 b, depicts an STM image of the frontier of a FeClTPP terrace from Figure 6.15 a. Although the image is a bit large scaled, the resolution of the STM is still enough to observe the molecules forming the terrace.

Figure 6.19 a shows the comparison between the normalized spectra obtained when the tip is placed on Ag(111) (Silver Curve) and on top of the PdTPP island (Blue Curve). Although the normalization process helps equalizing the overall spectral intensities, both curves are still not completely equivalent. Figure 6.20 shows the spectral dependence of such magnitude, in which we can make some observations. Firstly, and visible in Figure 6.19 a, when the tip locates on top of the PdTPP islands during tunnel excitation, the overall intensity of the plasmonic electroluminescence enhances. Secondly, $\mathrm{\Delta}P/P$ is mostly flat for relatively small photon energies and starts increasing at approximately 1.95 eV. Moreover, we can observe a peak at about 2.12 eV. We tentatively attribute this difference in energy to the screening effect of the metallic substrate. To rule out the possible effect of the tip, we have repeated the experiment with a different one. To rule out the possible effect of the tip, we have repeated the experiment with a different one. Figure 6.21 a shows the renormalized electroluminescence spectra recorded with both tips, the one from the previous analysis (Tip 1-Blue Curve), and the new one (Tip 2-Red Curve). Although the peak center on both curves is not significantly affected, the curve of Tip 2 has lower intensity in the high energy region, but a higher one towards the infrared. Although the values are not identical, they are very close and the overall spectral shape is identical, including the peak at 2.12 eV. We are thus confident that our analysis is revealing spectral features that correspond to the optical properties of the molecules directly adsorbed on metal surfaces. texto:
Chapter 6: Adsorption and emission effects of PdTPP and FeClTPP on noble metal surfaces > 6.5 Conclusions

In this chapter we have characterized the adsorption and electronic structure of two related molecules, PdTPP and FeClTPP. Both consist of a polyaromatic porphyrin moiety with peripheral phenyl groups that lift the aromatic plane from the metal surface, providing some insulation. Moreover, both have a non-planar structure due to the metallic center at the porphyrin core which enables optical processes with out-of-plane transition dipoles. By comparing the normalized plasmonic electroluminescence spectra in bare metallic surfaces and molecule-covered areas, we have found spectral differences in the energy range that would correspond to the absorption spectra of both molecules. Thus, we believe that with this normalization method we can obtain the equivalent to optical absorption spectra with atomic resolution and for molecules in direct contact with the metal surface.

seccion: Chapter 7: General Conclusions
texto:
Chapter 7: General Conclusions

General Conclusions In this thesis, we studied the optical and electronic properties of organic molecules inside plasmonic nanojunctions formed by an STM tip and a metallic surface (Au(111) or Ag(111)) or dielectric surface (NaCl on the previous metals). Also, we studied the interaction of fullertubes on the previous surfaces. The general conclusions of the work presented in this thesis can be divided in three sections. Firstly, for the first time we have studied the structural and electronic properties of C~90~ molecules by means of STM imaging and spectroscopy. STM images of C~90~ islands on noble metal surfaces (Ag(111) and Au(111)) revealed a rhomboidal self-assembly with the long axis of the molecules parallel to the surface which depicts a molecule-substrate interaction stronger than the molecule-molecule interaction. This behavior is similar to a fullerene molecule.

This behavior is similar to a fullerene molecule. Moreover, due to the resolution of the STM images we were able to create some lattice models for the molecules on both metallic surfaces. For C~90~/Ag(111), the lattice vectors of the islands of C~90~ follow an integer relation with respect the lattice vectors of the Ag(111) surface. In the case of the C~90~/Au(111) experiments, the relation between the lattice vector of the C~90~ molecule's island and the Au(111) surface follows approximately the same integer relation as the previous metal.

Furthermore, Density Functional Theory calculations along with our experimental results, revealed that we can classify the electronic states of the fullertubes according to their resemblance with the electronic structure of the infinite [5,5]-SWCNT. We were able to define some fullertube orbitals as the discretized version of the delocalized Bloch states of the infinite CNT band due to strong quantum confinement, suggesting a nanotube-like electronic structure. Also, other fullertube orbitals were more localized at its edges which indicated an origin unrelated to quantum confinement of infinite CNT bands and hence, suggesting a fullerene-like electronic structure. Finally, we have developed a variety of recipes for the fabrication of C~90~ nanostructures and studied their crystalline and electronic structures on different substrates. Thus, weaker (or stronger) molecule-substrate interaction with respect the intermolecular interaction can lead to a fullerene (or CNT) like behavior.

The necessity to measure at constant current causes a blue shift on the normalized spectra of both BPEA and BPEN with respect the metallic surface as a change in the distance between the tip and the sample. Finally, by attending to the changes of the spectral distribution of the normalized intensities we can study the optical properties of individual organic molecules on direct metallic surfaces avoiding the necessity of an insulating material in between both. Moreover, we could not extract optical information from individual molecules on metals by direct excitation of molecular luminescence due to the quenching effect of the metal. However, as there is a coupling between the excitonic modes of the BPEA and BPEN molecules and the plasmonic modes of the metal, by studying the changes on these plasmonic modes caused by the molecules, we can study the optical properties of the very same molecule.

Finally, regarding future lines of work on our laboratory, we are planning to prepare silver tips enhancing the overlap with the absorption spectra of our molecules by exciting plasmonic modes higher in energy than golden tips. Finally, we have characterized the adsorption and electronic structure of the two related molecules PdTPP and FeClTPP. Regarding its structure they both present a polyaromatic porphyrin moiety with peripheral phenyl groups that lift the aromatic plane from the metal surface. These phenyl groups provide the molecule with some insulation from the metallic surface where it adsorbs. Also, due to the metallic center at the porphyrin core both molecules present a non-planar structure. Thus, it enables optical processes with out-of-plane transition dipoles.

Chapter 7: General Conclusions

The results obtained on these experiments with PdTPP and FeClTPP adsorbed on both Ag(111) and Au(111) open the way to optical characterization with atomic resolution and without the need for electrical insulation. Hence, making it more useful for a broad range of applications ranging from the chemical characterization of on-surface synthesized molecules to new pathways to explore strong light -matter coupling. In Summary, the results presented in this thesis contribute to the understanding of the boundaries between fullerenes and carbon nanotubes structures, with the crystalline and electronic characterization of fullertubes and to the field of optoelectronics with the investigation of the changes in the plasmonic modes on nano-cavities with organic molecules inside them.
